I heard the ex-parte final arguments advanced by learned counsel for the petitioner and also perused the evidence and other materials placed on record.

My findings on the issues are as under:
ISSUE NO.1

Whether petitioner suffered injuries during the accident occurred on 16.09.2018 at about 12:30 hours, in front of J&K Pocket, Seemapuri Road, Dilshad Garden, Delhi, due to rash and negligent driving of the vehicle bearing no.
DL5SU-8872, being driven by respondent no.1/ driver? OPP 11.

It is seen that the petitioner got himself examined as PW1 and testified by way of his affidavit Ex.PW1/A on the lines of the FIR which he had got lodged on the basis of his statement made to police. PW1/ injured deposed that on 16.09.2018 at about 12:30 p.m., while he was crossing the road near Mother Dairy, in front of J & K Pocket, Dilshad Garden, Delhi, a motorcycle (make-Discover)
bearing registration no. DL5SU-8872, being driven by the respondent no.1 Faishal at a fast speed and carelessly, came from Kalandar Colony side and hit him, due to which he (petitioner) fell down on the road and received injuries.
PW1 stated that he was shifted to GTB Hospital, Delhi, where his MLC was prepared and further treatment was done.

Though the petitioner (PW1) was cross- examined by learned counsel for the respondents, however, it is seen that nothing has come during entire cross-examination of PW1, which may demolish his testimony.
The suggestion was given to PW1 that motorcycle of the respondents has been falsely implicated in the present case in order to extort money, which was promptly denied by the witness.

Thus, the testimony of the petitioner has ____________________________________________________________ MACT no.
675/2018, Saddik v. Faisal & Anr. 5 of 21 Pages remained uncontroverted, which deserves to be accepted on its face value itself in the absence of any defence brought or proved on record by the respondent side in support of their plea of false implication.

Further, on perusal of the DAR Ex.PW1/D (colly), this Tribunal finds that the information of the accident was received by the police immediately after the accident on 16.09.2018, which was reduced into writing vide DD no.14A, dated 16.09.2018.

Though the FIR was registered after two days on 18.09.2018, however, the explanation of such delay has been clearly given by the injured in the FIR itself that the injured could not give his statement on the date of accident itself as he was having severe pain due to injuries and that talks of settlement were also going on with the respondent no.1 but since respondent has refused to get him treated, he got his statement recorded on 18.09.2018 seeking legal action against the respondent no.1.

Furthermore, the FIR reveals that after hitting the injured, the driver/ respondent no.1 had fallen down along with the motorcycle and also sustained injuries and said fact is corroborated from the MLC of the injured and MLC of the respondent no.1 Faisal, which were prepared at GTB Hospital on 16.09.2018 vide MLC no.4872/30/18 and MLC no.6856/39/18, respectively, as per FIR and charge-sheet.
Moreover, the mechanical inspection report of the offending vehicle at page no.27 of the DAR clearly shows the accidental damages received by the offending vehicle.

The Site Plan of the place of the accident which is part of the DAR, also supports the manner of accident, as per version of the injured/
petitioner.

Apart from above, there is no challenge from the respondent/ driver of the offending vehicle to the version of the petitioner with respect to the manner of accident and involvement of the offending vehicle in accident.

The respondent was the best witness, who could have stepped into the witness box to challenge the testimony of the injured (PW1) regarding the above accident and its manner but neither he filed a reply to the claim petition nor preferred to enter into the witness box during the course of inquiry.

Thus, an adverse inference is liable to be drawn against him to the effect that the accident in question occurred due to rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle by him in view of the law laid down in case of Cholamaandalam M.S. General Insurance Company Ltd. v.
Kamlesh, 2009(3) AD (Delhi) 310.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Vidhyadhar v. Manikrao, (1999) 3 SCC 573 has observed that:
"17. Where a party to the suit does not appear in the witness box and states his own case on oath and does not offer himself to be cross-examined by the other side, a presumption would arise that the case set up by him is not correct....".

the petitioner sustained grievous injuries.

It is settled proposition of law that in an action founded on the principle of fault liability, the proof of rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle is sine-qua-non.
However, the standard of proof is not as strict as applied in criminal cases and evidence is to be tested on the touchstone of the preponderance of probabilities.
Holistic view is to be taken while dealing with the Claim Petition based upon negligence.
Strict rules of evidence are not applicable in an inquiry conducted by the Claims Tribunal.

However, that does not mean that a Tribunal which has been approached with a claim for compensation under the Motor Vehicle Act should ignore all basic principles of law in determining the claim for compensation.
The relevant provisions of the Act are not intended to jettison all principles of law relating to a claim for compensation which is still based on a tortious liability.

Reference may be made to the judgments titled as; New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Sakshi Bhutani & Others., MAC APP. No. 550/2011 decided on 02.07.2012, Bimla Devi & Others v.
Himachal Road Transport Corporation & Others (2009) 13 SC 530, Parmeshwari v. Amirchand &
Others 2011 (1) SCR 1096 & Mangla Ram v. Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. & Others 2018, Law Suit (SC) 303, Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Meena Variyal & Ors., (2007) 5 SCC 428.
17.

COMPUTATION OF COMPENSATION 18. Section 168 of M.V. Act, 1988 enjoins upon the claim Tribunal to hold an inquiry into the claim to make an award determining the amount of compensation, which appears to be just and reasonable.
As per settled law, compensation is not expected to be a windfall or a bonanza nor it should be a pittance.
"Just compensation" cannot be equated with bonanza but it suggests application of fair and equitable principles and reasonable approach of the Tribunal while awarding the compensation.
This reasonableness must be on a large peripheral field.

A man is not compensated for the physical injury which he might have received in the accident caused by the motor vehicle in a public place, rather he is compensated for the loss which he suffers as a result of the injury, he suffered in the accident.
[Ref. Yadava Kumar v. National Insurance Co. Ltd., (2010) 10 SCC 34; Raj Kumar v. Ajay Kumar, (2011) 1 SCC 343; Puttamma v. K.L. Narayana Reddy, (2013) 15 SCC 45].

sentences.text: 19. The present claim petition pertains to injury and scope of compensation in injury cases has been considered by Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as Mr. R.D. Hattangadi v. M/S Pest Control (India) Pvt. Ltd., 1995 AIR 755.

The relevant extract is as under:
"Broadly speaking while fixing an amount of compensation payable to a victim of an accident, the damages have to be assessed separately as pecuniary ____________________________________________________________ MACT no. 675/2018, Saddik v. Faisal & Anr. 9 of 21 Pages damages and special damages.

Pecuniary damages are those which the victim has actually incurred and Dar - Saddik vs Faishal on 10 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/39681989/
5 which is capable of being calculated in terms of money-, whereas non-pecuniary damages are those which are incapable of being assessed by arithmetical calculations.

In order to appreciate two concepts pecuniary damages may, include expenses incurred by the claimant: (i) medical attendance;
(ii) loss of earning of profit up to the date of trial; (iii) other material losses.
20. Further, in Raj Kumar v. Ajay Kumar & another (2011) 1 SCC 343, Hon'ble Supreme Court of India laid down general principles for computation of compensation in injury cases.

entities.text: Raj Kumar v. Ajay Kumar & another (2011) 1 SCC 343
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The relevant paras of the judgment are reproduced as under:
"4. The provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 ("the Act", for short) makes it clear that the award must be just, which means that compensation should, to the extent possible, fully and adequately restore the claimant to the position prior to the accident.
The object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner.

The court or the Tribunal shall have to assess the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation or fancy, though some conjecture with reference to the nature of disability and its consequences, is inevitable.
A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury.

This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have earned.

The heads under which compensation is awarded in personal injury cases are the following:
Pecuniary Damages (special damages)
(i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalization, medicines, transportation,
nourishing food and miscellaneous expenditure.

Dar - Saddik vs Faishal on 10 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/39681989/
6

(ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured, comprising:
(a) Loss of earning during the period of treatment.
(b) Loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability.
(iii) Future medical expenses.

Non-Pecuniary Damages (general damages)
(iv) Damages to pain, suffering and trauma as a consequence of the injuries.
(v) Loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage)
(vi) Loss of expectation of life (shortening of normal longevity).

In routine personal injury cases, compensation will be awarded only under heads (i), (ii)(a) and (iv).
It is only in serious cases of injury, where there is specific medical evidence corroborating the evidence of the claimant, that compensation will be granted under any of the heads (ii) (b), (iii), (v)
and (vi) relating to loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability, future medical expenses, loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage) and loss of expectation of life."
21.

23.
The discharge summary (Ex.PW1/C) shows that the petitioner remained admitted in GTB Hospital, Delhi from 16.09.2018 to 25.09.2018.

Further, the discharge summary reveals that he was diagnosed to have suffered multiple fractures i.e.
"closed fracture of DER (B/L) with PIP joint dislocation of the little finger with right Dar - Saddik vs Faishal on 10 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/39681989/

24. The injured/ petitioner (PW1) deposed that at the time of the accident, he was working as a labourer and was earning Rs.15,000/-
per month.

It is evident that petitioner has not placed on record any supporting document to substantiate his claim with respect to his occupation and income nor he filed any document to show h i s e d u c a t i o n . T h e A d h a a r C a r d o f t h e p e t i t i o n e r , w h i c h h a s b e e n p r o v e d ____________________________________________________________ MACT no.
675/2018, Saddik v. Faisal & Anr. 12 of 21 Pages on record as Ex.PW1/A
, reflects the residential address of the petitioner as that of Delhi.

Thus, in the absence of any documentary evidence regarding the income and education of the petitioner, his income has to be assessed at par with minimum wages applicable to unskilled category workers of Delhi on the date of accident (16.09.2018), which were Rs.13,896/- per month.
Accordingly, a sum of Rs.13,896/- is granted to the petitioner on account of loss of income of one month during treatment.

Loss of Future Earnings Due to Disability:
25.
It is not the case of the injured/ petitioner that injuries caused to him in the accident resulted into any kind of permanent disability, which would affect his future earnings.
Hence, petitioner is not entitled to any compensation under this head.

Special Diet, Conveyance & Attendant Charges:
26.
Though, the petitioner (PW1) has not specified in his affidavit of evidence the expenses which he incurred on special diet, transportation and as attendant charges during his treatment.

However, considering the multiple fractures which the petitioner sustained in the accident and the surgery (ORIF with 2 CCS of 60 mm and 55 mm with CR+B/E Cast B/L) done during hospitalization on 22.09.2018, it may be safely inferred that the petitioner must have spent a reasonable amount on high-rich protein diet for the purpose of early recovery, especially post surgery as well as for visiting the hospital for his further treatment.

Also, it cannot be ignored that h i s f a m i l y m e m b e r s m u s t h a v e s p e n t t h e i r c o n s i d e r a b l e t i m e i n a t t e n d i n g ____________________________________________________________ MACT no.
675/2018, Saddik v. Faisal & Anr. 13 of 21 Pages him during his treatment (refer: (Refer : DTC & Ors Vs. Lalita, 1983 ACJ 253).

In view of this Tribunal, a sum of Rs.10,000/- each for special diet,
conveyance and attendant charges would be just and fair compensation to the petitioner.
Hence, a total sum of Rs.30,000/- is awarded to the petitioner under this head.

NON PECUNIARY DAMAGES:
Pain & Sufferings:

27 . The discharge summary shows that after sustaining injuries in the accident on 16.09.2018, the petitioner remained hospitalized in GTB Hospital for 10 days i.e.,
from 16.09.2018 to 25.09.2018.

The discharge summary further reveals that the petitioner was diagnosed to have suffered "closed fracture of DER (B/L) with PIP joint dislocation of the little finger with right proximal tibia fracture with fractures of distal tibia (right)" and for treatment of said injuries, he was operated upon on 22.09.2018 when "ORIF with 2 CCS of 60 mm and 55 mm with CR+B/E Cast B/L"
was done.

Though no further treatment record has been filed but considering the nature of injuries, it may be safely assumed that the petitioner would have also undergone OPD treatment after being discharged from the hospital.

Thus, it is clear from the record that due to the injuries suffered in the accident, the petitioner must have gone through considerable pain and suffering during his treatment and therefore, a sum of Rs.25,000/- is awarded to the petitioner under this head.
28.

LIABILITY 31.
Now, the question arises as to which of the respondents is liable to pay the compensation amount.

Admittedly, the offending vehicle was not insured at the time of accident and therefore, the respondent no.1 being driver of the offending vehicle is the principal tortfeasor whereas, respondent no.2 being the owner would have the vicarious liability.
Accordingly, the respondent nos. 1 and 2 would have been liable to pay the compensation amount to the petitioner and their liability would have been joint and several.

opennyai_summary.facts:
During the investigation, the offending vehicle was found uninsured.
Moreover, the mechanical inspection report of the offending vehicle at page no.27 of the DAR clearly shows the accidental damages received by the offending vehicle.
The respondent was the best witness, who could have stepped into the witness box to challenge the testimony of the injured (PW1) regarding the above accident and its manner but neither he filed a reply to the claim petition nor preferred to enter into the witness box during the course of inquiry.
opennyai_summary.issue:
5. On completion of proceedings, vide order dated 14.01.2019, following issues were framed:
i) Whether petitioner suffered injuries during the accident occurred on 16.09.2018 at about 12:30 hours, in front of J&K Pocket, Seemapuri Road, Dilshad Garden, Delhi,
due to rash and negligent driving of the vehicle bearing no. DL5SU-8872, being driven by respondent no.1/ driver?

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
Apart from above, there is no challenge from the respondent/ driver of the offending vehicle to the version of the petitioner with respect to the manner of accident and involvement of the offending vehicle in accident.
Thus, an adverse inference is liable to be drawn against him to the effect that the accident in question occurred due to rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle by him in view of the law laid down in case of Cholamaandalam M.S. General Insurance Company Ltd. v.
Kamlesh, 2009(3) AD (Delhi) 310.
It is settled proposition of law that in an action founded on the principle of fault liability, the proof of rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle is sine-qua-non.
However, the standard of proof is not as strict as applied in criminal cases and evidence is to be tested on the touchstone of the preponderance of probabilities.
Holistic view is to be taken while dealing with the Claim Petition based upon negligence.
Strict rules of evidence are not applicable in an inquiry conducted by the Claims Tribunal.
However, that does not mean that a Tribunal which has been approached with a claim for compensation under the Motor Vehicle Act should ignore all basic principles of law in determining the claim for compensation.
The relevant provisions of the Act are not intended to jettison all principles of law relating to a claim for compensation which is still based on a tortious liability.
Reference may be made to the judgments titled as; New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Sakshi Bhutani & Others., MAC APP. No. 550/2011 decided on 02.07.2012, Bimla Devi & Others v.
Himachal Road Transport Corporation & Others (2009) 13 SC 530, Parmeshwari v. Amirchand &
Others 2011 (1) SCR 1096 & Mangla Ram v. Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. & Others 2018, Law Suit (SC) 303, Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Meena Variyal & Ors., (2007) 5 SCC 428.
17.
As per settled law, compensation is not expected to be a windfall or a bonanza nor it should be a pittance.
"Just compensation" cannot be equated with bonanza but it suggests application of fair and equitable principles and reasonable approach of the Tribunal while awarding the compensation.
This reasonableness must be on a large peripheral field.
A man is not compensated for the physical injury which he might have received in the accident caused by the motor vehicle in a public place, rather he is compensated for the loss which he suffers as a result of the injury, he suffered in the accident.
[Ref. Yadava Kumar v. National Insurance Co. Ltd., (2010) 10 SCC 34; Raj Kumar v. Ajay Kumar, (2011) 1 SCC 343; Puttamma v. K.L. Narayana Reddy, (2013) 15 SCC 45].
20. Further, in Raj Kumar v. Ajay Kumar & another (2011) 1 SCC 343, Hon'ble Supreme Court of India laid down general principles for computation of compensation in injury cases.
Thus, in the absence of any documentary evidence regarding the income and education of the petitioner, his income has to be assessed at par with minimum wages applicable to unskilled category workers of Delhi on the date of accident (16.09.2018), which were Rs.13,896/- per month.
Accordingly, a sum of Rs.13,896/- is granted to the petitioner on account of loss of income of one month during treatment.
Loss of Future Earnings Due to Disability:
25.
It is not the case of the injured/ petitioner that injuries caused to him in the accident resulted into any kind of permanent disability, which would affect his future earnings.
Hence, petitioner is not entitled to any compensation under this head.
However, considering the multiple fractures which the petitioner sustained in the accident and the surgery (ORIF with 2 CCS of 60 mm and 55 mm with CR+B/E Cast B/L) done during hospitalization on 22.09.2018, it may be safely inferred that the petitioner must have spent a reasonable amount on high-rich protein diet for the purpose of early recovery, especially post surgery as well as for visiting the hospital for his further treatment.
In view of this Tribunal, a sum of Rs.10,000/- each for special diet,
conveyance and attendant charges would be just and fair compensation to the petitioner.

LIABILITY 31.
Admittedly, the offending vehicle was not insured at the time of accident and therefore, the respondent no.1 being driver of the offending vehicle is the principal tortfeasor whereas, respondent no.2 being the owner would have the vicarious liability.
Accordingly, the respondent nos. 1 and 2 would have been liable to pay the compensation amount to the petitioner and their liability would have been joint and several.
In the light of the above discussion, the present claim petition is allowed.
Accordingly, the following award is passed:
